extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, administrative-law theorists, political theorists, and policymakers interested in democratic institutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating legal and institutional reforms to embody agonistic democratic theory within the administrative state — i.e., how agencies, rules, and processes can preserve contestation and manage conflict. Focuses on normative criteria for institutions that seek to make conflict productive rather than suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept ineradicable disagreement (agonism core)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agonism rejects the assumption that conflict can or should be extinguished in lawmaking; the process of contestation itself is intrinsically valuable and legitimacy stems from the opportunity to resist settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion emphasizes that institutions should 'take ineradicable disagreement seriously.' Anti-patterns: treating democracy solely as a method to produce a single, settled 'will' of the demos or privileging consensus to the exclusion of persistent minorities. Examples cited: Mouffe, Honig; empirical support from cases where agonistic approaches reduce destructive antagonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an enduring space for contestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should 'create a space in which [agonistic] confrontation is kept open, power relations are always being put into question and no victory can be final.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalizes agonism as institutional design: spaces must remain permanently contestable rather than allowing definitive closures. Examples: democratic constitutionalism and recurring patterns of resistance; anti-patterns include institutional closure and ossification of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design rules to be contingent, provisional, and responsive
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and institutional rules should be contingent, provisional, and responsive to contestation rather than rigid, permanent commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires trading some traditional 'rule of law' values (like maximal stability) for temporal flexibility. Guidance: encourage provisional formulations and processes that invite reconsideration; beware of undermining intelligibility or practicability unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide effective mechanisms for agenda access and reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the demos must have effective ways of coercing political institutions to add items to the agenda and to reconsider any and all policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should enable agenda-setting by challengers and routine reconsideration of policy (preventing ossification). Examples: channels for countermobilization and 'constituent moments' that force reexamination of the status quo; anti-pattern: systems that lock policies in place with high barriers to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable institutions to effectuate change while permitting countermobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: When a decision changes the status quo, institutions must be free to effectuate that decision even if it creates new winners and losers, because agonistic institutions rely on political countermobilization against the new status quo to check bad decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should allow both decisive action and subsequent contestation rather than neutralizing opponents through procedural assimilation. Anti-pattern: decisions that are irreversible or that eliminate avenues for challengers to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumscribe the inviolability of law to allow agonistic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The inviolability of law must be circumscribed when agonistic claims advance; law must be capable of facilitating 'constituent moments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion accepts deliberate limits on legal inviolability to permit democratic claims that unsettle settled arrangements. Tradeoffs: may conflict with Fullerian rule-of-law desiderata (consistency, stability). Guidance: design circumscription narrowly and procedurally to avoid arbitrary instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster inclusion, secure plurality, and safeguard differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Agonistic institutions should foster inclusion, secure plurality, and safeguard differences so that adversaries can coexist as 'friendly enemies' rather than descend into antagonism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures should protect marginalized voices and create democratic outlets for contestation; examples include making space for subaltern counterpublics and protecting nonmajoritarian speech forms. Anti-pattern: purported consensus that excludes persistent minorities, producing alienation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate conflict to defuse antagonism and prevent violence
rubrics_metrics.description: The design aim is to defuse potential antagonism by recognizing and embracing conflict in regulated ways that prevent escalation into destructive antagonism or civil strife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize mechanisms that channel hostility into nonviolent political contestation. Empirical rationale: agonistic approaches have been linked to reduced destructive antagonism in case studies (e.g., truth and reconciliation, participatory planning). Anti-patterns: institutional designs that either suppress conflict (risking later antagonism) or amplify it without safeguards (risking polarization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include safeguards against hyperpoliticization and gridlock
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutionalization must be attentive to pathologies of agonism—hyperpoliticization, polarization, gridlock—and include institutional safeguards to prevent them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that reflexive contestation can produce pathologies; design should balance openness to contestation with procedural checks that prevent paralysis or violent factionalization. Examples: contingent rules, procedural limiters, institutional channels for mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden legitimate communicative forms in deliberative forums
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberative processes compatible with agonism should permit a wider range of discursive moves (e.g., greeting, rhetoric, storytelling) rather than narrowly-defined 'ideal speech' reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages inclusion of culturally situated voices and rhetorical forms to avoid artificial exclusion of ordinary citizens. Reference: Iris Marion Young's communicative democracy. Anti-patterns: deliberative forums that tightly control legitimate speech forms and thereby exclude perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize law to prioritize intelligibility, practicability, and congruence when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize tradeoffs between rule-of-law values (consistency, stability) and other legal goods (intelligibility, practicability, congruence); agonistic institutionalization may sacrifice some stability to achieve democratic responsiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should consciously weigh and justify tradeoffs; seek to maintain the 'morality of law' by preserving intelligibility and practicability even when allowing temporal instability. Anti-pattern: sacrificing intelligibility or practicability for contestability in ways that make law unintelligible or unworkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow democratic constitutionalism and 'unsettlement' across legal domains
rubrics_metrics.description: The agonistic ethic supports democratic constitutionalism: citizens must have rights to make claims about constitutional meaning and to oppose government through constitutional lawmaking, electoral politics, and civil society; 'unsettlement' is a virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion extends agonistic institutionalization beyond constitutional law into other legal areas (including administrative law). Guidance: cultivate recurring patterns of resistance and institutional recognition of those patterns as legitimate democratic inputs. Anti-pattern: legal systems that treat all departures from settled law as illegitimate without democratic space for contestation.
